title: High blood pressure: cut salt in Malaysian food without losing the taste
intro: Malaysian food is really sedap, but a lot of it is high in salt. Kicap (soy sauce), sauces, ikan masin, budu, belacan and seasoning powder all contain salt. If you have high blood pressure, cutting down on salt can help, together with your doctor's treatment. The good news is you can still eat tasty food. Your tongue usually gets used to less salty food within a few weeks.

sections.p: Health guidelines usually suggest no more than about one teaspoon of salt a day. That includes the salt in kicap, sauces and food you buy. Many people take much more without realising. This is an estimate, not an exact measurement.

Noodle soup, curry gravy, chilli sauce, oyster sauce, kicap, ikan masin, salted eggs, sausages, nuggets, keropok and canned food are usually high in salt. Instant noodles are also high in salt, especially the seasoning packet. Have them less often. You don't have to cut them out completely.

At a noodle stall, drink only half the soup. At nasi campur, ask for a little kuah (gravy) or put it on the side of the plate. Dip less into sauces and kicap. Choose grilled, steamed or clear soup dishes more often. Add vegetables and fruit for balance.

Use shallots, garlic, ginger, serai, lengkuas, daun kesum, kaffir lime leaves and black pepper. A squeeze of lime or asam jawa can lift the flavour. Curry spices and turmeric also help. Reduce the salt in your recipes little by little so your family won't notice.
Walking every day, chair exercises and wall push-ups can help heart health. Avoid holding your breath when you exercise. Breathe normally. If you feel dizzy or have chest pain, stop and rest.

action: Drink only half the soup when you eat noodles or soup outside.
Taste your food first before adding kicap or salt.
Reduce the salt in home cooking a little every week.
Replace some of the seasoning with lime, serai, ginger or black pepper.
Walk 10 to 20 minutes a day, as much as you can manage.
doctor: See your doctor first if you have kidney disease, heart disease, or are taking blood pressure medicine, because some salt substitutes and high-potassium foods may not be suitable for you. Get urgent treatment if you suddenly have a severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, blurred vision, or weakness on one side of the body. Don't change or stop your medicine on your own, even if your readings are already good. Discuss with your doctor.

faq.q: Is rock salt or sea salt healthier?
faq.a: All types of salt contain sodium. Their effect on blood pressure is about the same. What matters is the amount, not the type.

faq.q: My blood pressure reading is normal now. Can I stop my medicine?
faq.a: Don't stop on your own. The good reading may be because the medicine is working. Talk to your doctor if you feel you want to change anything.

faq.q: Less salty food doesn't taste good. What should I do?
faq.a: Cut down slowly. Your tongue usually starts getting used to it within a few weeks. Add flavour with herbs, spices, lime and onions so your food stays tasty.
